procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court dated 25.7.1983, which was an interim order pending consideration of an appeal filed against the order of a learned Single Judge of that High Court dated 18.7.1983.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Respondents 1 to 4 filed an application before the Sub-Divisional Magistrate under s. 145(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to recall an ex parte order. The Magistrate adjourned the application.
2. Respondents 1 to 4 moved a revision application under the Criminal Revisional Jurisdiction of the High Court and obtained a stay of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate's order of April 26, 1983. This revision application is still pending.
3. Respondents 1 to 4 applied to be impleaded as parties to Suit No. 2024 of 1952 and for staying and setting aside the High Court's orders dated 24.5.1983 and 26.5.1983. This application came before Monjula Bose, J.
4. The learned Single Judge dismissed their application on 18.7.1983.
5. Respondents 1 to 4 filed an appeal (Appeal No. 271 of 1983) against the order of the learned Single Judge dated 18.7.1983.
6. A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court made an interim order on 25.7.1983 in the appeal filed by Respondents 1 to 4.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the interim order of the Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court dated 25.7.1983.

directions: The two orders of the learned Judge dated May 24, 1983 and May 26, 1983 are vacated.
The impugned order dated July 18, 1983 is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was a concluded and confirmed sale in favour of the appellant when the acceptance of the offer was conditional and amounted to a counter-offer.

facts: The appellant made an offer to purchase property.
The receiver's acceptance of the offer was made subject to a new condition: that the appellant would purchase the property subject to pending litigation.
This condition was not part of the appellant's original offer.
The appellant did not provide a fresh acceptance of this new condition.
The appellant also failed to pay the balance amount of Rs. 3 lakhs as required.
law: For a contract to be concluded, an acceptance of an offer must be absolute and unconditional.
An acceptance that imposes a new condition is not a valid acceptance but is considered a counter-offer.
A counter-offer must be accepted by the original offeror to form a binding contract.
application: The Court, agreeing with the Division Bench, determined that the receiver's acceptance was not absolute because it introduced the new condition regarding pending litigation.
This conditional acceptance was legally a counter-offer, not a final acceptance of the appellant's original offer.
Since the appellant never accepted this new counter-offer, no binding contract was ever formed.
The Court also noted that the appellant's failure to pay the balance amount further demonstrated that the sale had not become operative or been concluded.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim, concluding that there was no concluded and confirmed sale. The receiver's conditional acceptance was a counter-offer that the appellant never accepted, meaning a binding contract was never formed.

issue.issue_text: Whether proceedings under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure affect the title of the parties to the disputed premises.

law.quote: The Magistrate shall then, without reference to the merits Or the claims of any· of the claims of any of the parties to a right to possess the subject of the dispute... decide whether any and which of the.parties was, at the date of the order made by him under sub-section (I), in possession of the subject of dispute.

application.explanation: The Supreme Court explicitly stated that proceedings under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and any resulting orders do not affect the title of the parties to the disputed property.

application.explanation: The Court's reasoning is based on the limited scope of the proceeding as defined by the statute itself. Section 145(4) mandates that the Magistrate must decide the issue of possession 'without reference to the merits' of any party's claim to a 'right to possess' the property.
supporting_text: The Magistrate shall then, without reference to the merits ·Or the claims of any· of the claims of any of the parties to a right to possess the subject of the dispute...

application.explanation: Therefore, the inquiry is strictly confined to determining which party was in actual physical possession at a specific time to prevent a breach of the peace. It is a summary proceeding that does not, and cannot, adjudicate on the legal ownership or title to the property.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that proceedings under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure do not affect the title of the parties because the scope of such proceedings is statutorily limited to a summary determination of actual possession, explicitly excluding any consideration of the merits of the parties' legal right to possess or own the property.

issue.issue_text: In the absence of a concluded contract, whether the court could direct the disputed premises to be conveyed to the respondents for the benefit of 38 families on the grounds of social justice.

facts: The Supreme Court first determined that there was no concluded contract of sale in favor of the appellant. It considered this a "possible view" taken by the lower court and decided not to interfere with that finding.
The respondents, consisting of 38 families, were in actual possession of the disputed premises, even though their initial entry may have been illegitimate.
The respondents offered to purchase the property for Rs. 5,00,000, which was Rs. 1,00,000 more than the appellant's offer.
The property was considered to be in *custodia legis* (in the custody of the law), meaning the court retained power over its sale since the transaction had not been finalized.
law: The concept of social justice is an aspiration of the Constitution and can be a factor in judicial decisions, particularly to prevent the displacement of a large number of people.

When a property is under the court's control (*custodia legis*) and a sale has not been concluded, the court has the power to direct its officer to sell it to a party that would be more beneficial to the owners.
Courts can prioritize "substantial justice" over legal technicalities in certain circumstances.
application: The Court reasoned that since there was no concluded contract, it was not bound to approve the sale to the appellant.
It then applied the principle of social justice, stating that the factor of a large number of human beings being dislodged from their possession should influence the court's decision.
The Court acknowledged that while the families may have had "unclean hands" due to their initial entry, they were now seeking to be rehabilitated by purchasing the land at a competitive price.
The Court found that the lower court's decision achieved "substantial justice" by both securing a higher price for the property owners and allowing the 38 families to be rehabilitated.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that the property could be conveyed to the 38 families. It based its decision on the key finding that there was no concluded contract with the appellant, which allowed the court to prioritize social justice. This involved preventing the displacement of the families already in possession, especially since they were offering a higher price, thereby achieving a more just and beneficial outcome for all parties except the original potential buyer.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was a concluded and confirmed sale in favour of the appellant when the acceptance of the offer was conditional and amounted to a counter-offer.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that there was a concluded and confirmed sale in their favour, and that the lower court's order confirming the sale should be upheld.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that there was no concluded contract because the acceptance of the appellant's offer was conditional and therefore constituted a counter-offer, which was never accepted.

arguments.issue_text: Whether proceedings under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure affect the title of the parties to the disputed premises.
appellant_arguments: The appellant likely argued that proceedings under Section 145 CrPC are concerned only with possession to prevent a breach of peace and do not determine or affect the legal title to a property.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely raised the existence of Section 145 proceedings as a relevant factor in the dispute, implying that it complicated or had a bearing on the parties' rights to the property.

arguments.issue_text: In the absence of a concluded contract, whether the court could direct the disputed premises to be conveyed to the respondents for the benefit of 38 families on the grounds of social justice.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that without a concluded contract, the court had no legal basis to direct a conveyance to the respondents and that the property should either be sold to them as per the original bid or be put up for a new sale.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the court should exercise its equitable jurisdiction on the grounds of social justice to direct that the property be conveyed for the benefit of the 38 families involved, even in the absence of a concluded contract.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: While rendering social justice, no violence should be done to any established and well-known principles of law, but mere technicalities of law will not be allowed to stand in its way.
obiter: The court should move away from fine-spun technicalities and abstract rules to the recognition of human beings as human beings.

It is improper for the Supreme Court, in the exercise of the discretion vested under Article 136 of the Constitution, to interfere with a decision that has done substantial justice by setting aside technicalities.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In the absence of a concluded contract that would vest a legal right in the appellant, the court found it was justified in prioritizing social justice to solve a socio-economic problem. The court held that technicalities of law should not prevent a solution that provides housing for 38 families, especially when that solution is also financially advantageous to the property's owners and does not deprive any party of an existing legal right.
legal_tests_applied: Whether human needs can be fulfilled without deprivation of existing legal rights of any party concerned.
why_appellant_lost: The court determined there was no concluded contract in the appellant's favour, meaning the appellant did not possess an existing legal right to the property that was being deprived.
The appellant's claim was viewed as a 'technicality of law' that should not stand in the way of the court doing social justice for a larger group of people.

The court rejected the argument that accepting a higher offer in the name of social justice was an improper basis for its decision, framing it instead as the 'best course in the circumstances' to solve a human problem.
why_respondent_won: The court embraced a judicial philosophy where jurisprudence has shifted from 'technicalities and abstract rules to recognition of human being as human beings,' allowing it to address the housing needs of the 38 families.
The court found that doing 'social justice' was the paramount consideration, and this required selling the land to the petitioners and other residents.

The solution was seen as doing 'substantial justice' because it benefited a large number of people by preventing their eviction, while also providing a higher sale price (Rs. 1 lakh more) to the property owners.

Even though the residents were acknowledged to have 'unclean hands' due to their initial illegal entry, the court held they should not be denied the opportunity for rehabilitation at a competitive price.
policy_considerations: The concept of social justice is not foreign to legal justice or social well-being or benefit to the community rooted in the concept of justice in the 20th century.
Living accommodation is a human problem for vast millions in Our country.

In formulating the concept of justice, however, the inarticulate factor that large number of human beings should not be dislodged from their possession if it is otherwise possible to do so cannot but be a factor which must and should influence the minds of judges in the facts of this case.
Social justice is one of the aspirations of our Constitution.
